articles.title: Testing Einstein's laws from the bottom of the Mediterranean Sea
articles.description: Are the laws of physics truly the same everywhere in the universe? This fundamental principle, known as Lorentz invariance, lies at the heart of Einstein's theory of relativity. Yet some theories that seek to reconcile gravity with quantum physics suggest that it might not always hold. To investigate this possibility, researchers from the international KM3NeT collaboration analyzed 5,828 atmospheric neutrino candidate events detected by KM3NeT/ORCA, a neutrino telescope located deep in the Mediterranean Sea.

articles.title: One thought at a time
articles.description: One of my favorite books, which I actually happened to read for a class in high school, is Beloved by Toni Morrison. In addition to its captivating elements of magical realism, this book was my first exposure to stream-of-consciousness writing. This concept of writing is so freeing because you are allowed to rebel against all traditional rules of writing. No, you don't need to separate two independent clauses with a comma and a coordinating conjunction. In fact, run-ons are encouraged, and you can punctuate whenever or if ever. Truly, there is only one thing you need to do: start writing, and your train of thought will follow. I have to admit, it felt really abnormal and contradictory at first, especially in an English class. Ever since elementary school, we have been taught and instructed to follow all these grammar rules, and now you're telling me to disregard that? Nonetheless, whenever I read this style of writing, it may seem logically chaotic, but it's actually easy to follow because our minds embrace spontaneity. I have found it hard to write recently because it seems to be that all my mental energy has been going towards studying for the waves of exams that keep coming. There are times when I feel like I no longer have the capacity to process another thought. But our brains never tire. Never is there a time when there is no thought in our mind. And so, for this Voices article, I wanted to embody this style of writing. I don't have a theme or a concrete idea of what I want to write about, but I know the first step is to press some keys on a keyboard. A b c d e f g h i j k l My favorite way to end my days is with a warm cup of chamomile tea and some journaling. Especially after a day where everything seems to be going south, sipping on a warm concoction flavored with a hint of spice is all I need to re-ground myself to remember that everything is going to work out. The lingering warming sensation in your chest after you swallow is like an internal hug that you didn't know you needed. Before walking back to my room to journal, I have to stop by and look out the window in our common area. Looking down, you can see the Homewood Campus from a bird's-eye view, with trees enclosing it, but what catches my attention is what you see when you look far out into the horizon. A sea of lights, illuminating the skyscraper buildings downtown. There is something so calming and joyful about gazing at these lights upon the night sky. Who knew a hustling city could look just as serene as nature? Light has always been a physical representation of hope for me, and looking out, I can see with my own eyes how massive and alive the world is and how profound humanity can be. Sometimes, it's the little things in life like this that make it all worth living for. On the topic of little things, I have a small square-sized vision board propped up on my desk in my room, and one of the images on it is a compilation of lattes as a backdrop to the saying, "My cup overflows with blessings." I remember putting this image on there when I was making the board, because I love a good coffee, perhaps a little too much. I have successfully conditioned myself to need to have a caffeinated drink beside me as I study. I don't think it's inherently a bad thing, but it certainly isn't optimal either. It's certainly hard to walk into Brody and Mudd without getting a drink, though. Either way, there have definitely been days where coffee has been an absolute lifesaver, and there have been days where it was quite the opposite, and I was practically a sleepy zombie with a fast heart rate and jitters all day long. It's definitely something that I look forward to getting, but I know that I can't always rely on it to cure my sleep deprivation or mood. Other than the obvious solution, sleep, sometimes it's good conversations with friends (past midnight) that revive you. And then there's always food. Everyone has those meals that just have their own way of comforting and transporting you back "home." For me, it's definitely my grandmother's signature bone broth she would make for my cousins and I every Friday when we visited. Honestly, I wasn't always in the mood to drink it, but aside from its nutrients, I now know even just one teaspoon of it can bring back years of Friday night memories with my family. They're the reason why I'm here and why I want to keep living each day to the best of my ability. No day is the same, and every is truly a gift. I have recently been contemplating more about what defines my happiness: If I died tomorrow, would I be happy? And I want to continue to build my life around this question. One thing different from this exam season is that I definitely notice myself more at peace even though it has been more academically challenging. I think this comes from the fact that I know my identity as a human being and not a machine. Exams are a matter of performance and not always truly reflective of the knowledge you actually possess. Of course, the objective is to perform your best and have it be a true reflection of your knowledge, but sometimes they aren't, even though you gave it more than your all when studying. I know at the end of the day that I am not going to look back and care about the results and have that define me. Rather, it's the experiences of pushing my ability to focus and learn to the next level, the good times with friends and family, the moments where I am just observing and admiring the world and the other little everyday things in life. These are what matter most to me and always will. Catherine Chan is a sophomore studying Molecular and Cellular Biology as well as Public Health from Potomac, Md. Her column consists of reflections on various moments in her life, from the distant past to the current present, in pursuit of discovering the underlying impact they have on her life's story.

articles.title: To watch and watch for: Week of Nov. 1
articles.description: After a surely productive Halloweekend and the conclusion of Hoptoberfest always comes the onset of November and an imminent Thanksgiving. It is in between the spooky and the cuffing season that we find the rest of the genres neatly lined up for us to enjoy with friends and perhaps a dinner party to follow. If you're looking for an excuse to find reprieve from studying, a cozy JHMI read or an album to put on while getting ready in the morning, make sure to give this week's picks a chance! After premiering at the Venice International Film Festival this past September, the dark comedy spy thriller Wild Horse Nine is receiving its theatrical release this week. The film follows CIA agents Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell) on their deployment to Easter Island shortly before the military coup that would install Pinochet as President. As they uncover more details about their past and present situations, things seem to keep throwing their plans sideways. The movie is both deeply pensive and hilariously funny with a notable standout performance to watch for from Malkovich, who received Best Actor at Venice for his role. With the NBA season's recent tipoff, talks about greatness, potential and unfortunately, injuries have already taken off in full force. Even with all of the talent on display in the modern league, players and fans alike must always remember the giants whose shoulders the present game of basketball stands on, and the legendary coach Phil Jackson won't let us forget that. In the book Masters of the Game, close friends Jackson and former sports journalist Sam Smith discuss the stories of the all-time best players and the details that make up basketball history, both on and off the court. Unfortunately for fans of Bearface's contemplative parts on songs like SUMMER, the singer has kept his head down since BROCKHAMPTON's breakup in 2022. However, this July, he released K-Bar under the name Ciarán and has since been teasing songs from his upcoming album Róisín ever since. For fans looking for introspective alternative RnB and brilliantly harmonized falsettos, this long-awaited return might be just the release to scratch your brain. Too often, music listeners are allowed to see music as a solitary act. Streaming services allow us to pipe music directly into our own ears and allow us to forget what recommending your favorite to your friends was like. Artist in Residence Xavier "Seven" Walker is combating this by presenting the Black album Frequency Sound Library, a listening room focused on community building and growing roots in the sounds of Baltimore. Pop by on Nov. 5 to join in on the process of cultural creation! As always, you can also check out the extended list below for even more recommendations! articles.title: An admission of unkindness
articles.description: I fear kindness the way a cat fears water. One touch of that gaudy mask, and I want to scurry away. The showy nature behind it all functions as a party of porcelain dolls at a masquerade, with each disguise telling me about the lies that obscure the person responsible. Mostly, I fear the kindness in my own false image. My mask is likely much more extensive than yours, despite my best efforts at authenticity. And I am yet to figure out all the lies I've told. You should know what I mean. The pressurized camaraderie found in tight-knit social circles. An unspoken rule more binding than law to declare your agreement. It's all rather cultish. And I think we're all leaders whether we realize it or not. Of course, some more than others. Religious and political leaders concealing sexual abuse cases are completely different from your next-door neighbor who sends yearly Christmas cards talking shit about you. Still, it's just shit hitting the ever-revolving fan. Yet you can't really know what I am referring to. Even after reading this article, you still won't fully understand what I mean. Right now, as I write in a moment of rare serenity, I can only see it vaguely. That is because we will never truly grasp the depth of our own unkindness. Don't worry. You are probably a good person, maybe even a kind person. I promise I am not some pessimist who views every act of kindness as some elaborate scheme to get somewhere in the world. But let's be real. We are all thinkers. I wonder what your most intrusive thoughts are now. Are you like me? Wondering how some people still don't know sidewalk etiquette. Cursing a mom with a stroller who passed you on a half-marathon. Okay, maybe you didn't do those two, but I still think we're similar. In these moments of occasional insincerity, which I'll discuss soon, I always felt a vague illness creeping down my spine. I used to see this as my guilty conscience, and though that is not technically wrong, a better descriptor for me would be my own moral disillusionment. Before I go more in-depth on my own acts of cruelty, I should explain that I grew up in rural Minnesota. It is important to preface this by saying this is just my experience, and what happened there happens everywhere. Still, the stereotype of Midwesterners having a "fake kindness" rang especially true to me. I recall teachers with affirmations on their doors gossiping about past students. Moms and Dads at the local golf course saying the darnedest things as one went to the restroom. Friends and foes offering up a favor that you would be damned to accept. All within a day. Of course, I was an active participant. I just did not realize it then. My environment, which I considered entirely artificial, made for an easy scapegoat. On top of this, people, specifically my teachers, always said I was kind. They told my parents, who would then tell me with pride what they had heard. Any negative action I ever did was met with a reminder that it was uncharacteristic, and at my core, I was a good, kind person. When a positive trait is constantly applied to you, it is easy to believe you are incapable of the opposite. I'm sure most people believe they are kind because they want to believe they are good. But I believed I was kind because I never considered I couldn't be. I started waking up when I moved to Baltimore. Yes. I was aware of certain moral imperfections beforehand; a genuine apology wasn't foreign, but living in a different region gave me a completely different context. Without an environment to blame, or people who cast me as the kind one, it was difficult to brush off the mean thoughts that ran through my head about strangers and the gossip I partook in. As I ruminated on my ethical inadequacies, I began to understand that a moral shortcoming was not equivalent to a mistake or a mess-up. It was just an essential piece in discovering that I am both unkind and kind. I have never been the worst person in the world. And frankly, I like to think that despite everything in this article, I am still good. I would bring up examples to reinforce that claim because I worry that I come across as so many other things right now, but that would be frustratingly counterintuitive. While I don't claim them as core values, I acknowledge that anything opposite of kindness can be a trait of mine under the wrong circumstances. I am frightened that I won't always come to this understanding. What will likely happen is I will feel morally superior because someone else in my life does something much worse than whisper a bratty rumor. I write this article as an awakening from a spell we will likely fall under again. It is a reminder, saying that we are all capable of cruelty. Matthew Bohnsack is a freshman from Moose Lake, Minn., majoring in English.
